notes.title: Look at the building
notes.fact: Architectural works, sculpture and inscriptions can form part of cultural heritage.
notes.connection: Notice the temple-inspired gateways and carved surfaces. This environment is fictional, not a surveyed reconstruction.

notes.title: Repair needs knowledge
notes.fact: Unsuitable repairs can damage ceramics. Real pottery repair requires knowledge of the material and suitable techniques.
notes.connection: Joining the game's pot fragments is a simplified observation puzzle. It is not a guide to repairing real objects.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Care of Ceramics and Glass, Notes 5/1

notes.title: Keep a record
notes.fact: A professional inventory helps protect museum collections and prevent illicit trafficking.
notes.connection: Compare the vault ledger and the objects you recover. Recording what belongs in a collection matters.
notes.source: UNESCO, Museums and Collections Recommendation (2015), paragraph 8

notes.title: Water changes materials
notes.fact: Excavated objects can change after removal from the ground; salts and environmental conditions can damage archaeological materials.
notes.connection: The stepwell uses water as a game mechanism. Real excavated objects need specialist care, not a quick rinse.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Caring for archaeological collections

notes.title: Seeing and preserving
notes.fact: Light helps us see collections, but it can fade sensitive colours. Both brightness and exposure time matter.
notes.connection: The Sun Wall lets you observe light paths. Its mechanism is fictional; museum lighting also considers protection.
notes.source: Canadian Conservation Institute, Agent of Deterioration: Light, Ultraviolet and Infrared

notes.title: Pass heritage forward
notes.fact: Museums support education and cultural transmission, and citizens share responsibility for caring for heritage.
notes.connection: Return the fictional objects to their community. The recovery story is an invented adventure, not a historical event.
notes.source: UNESCO, Museums and Collections Recommendation (2015), paragraph 2

notes.title: Craft is also knowledge
notes.fact: Traditional craftsmanship includes the skills and knowledge used to make objects, not just the finished products.
notes.connection: The fictional market places dyers, potters and brass workers beside their tools. Observe the people and processes as well as the goods.

notes.title: Skills pass between people
notes.fact: Living heritage depends on people passing knowledge and skills from person to person and between generations.
notes.connection: Tea-lane neighbours share a working space. This invented market illustrates a living community rather than a collection of treasures.
